papers.title: ProlateNet: Sampling-rate transfer of convolutional networks with a weights-only certificate for physiological signals
papers.abstract: A central goal of physiological signal analysis is to train a model once and deploy it across recording systems. However, these systems sample EEG and ECG at different rates, and a network trained at one rate loses accuracy at the others. Continuous-kernel networks were built to solve this problem, but published ones still fail at unseen rates, and no existing method can certify a trained model before deployment. In this study, we propose ProlateNet, which builds kernels from prolate spheroidal wave functions to suppress aliasing across sampling rates and certifies a trained model from its weights alone. Across fourteen first-layer designs trained at one rate on three public EEG and ECG datasets, the published continuous-kernel layers FlexConv and sampling-frequency-independent (SFI) convolution show mean worst drops of 0.18 and 0.35 macro-F1 on SEED. ProlateNet is the only design that is stable and accurate on all three datasets with an error bound fixed before training, and its mean worst drop is at most 0.003. Without target-rate recordings, its certificate ranks the continuous-kernel designs on SEED by measured transfer with Spearman {rho} = 0.92, against 0.68 for energy above the training Nyquist frequency. Overall, ProlateNet shows that controlling aliasing enables convolutional networks to transfer across sampling rates and provides principled guidance for building physiological signal models that are trained once and deployed across recording systems.

papers.title: Dissociable patterns of neurophysiological alterations during guided search in schizophrenia and autism: Evidence from fixation-related potentials, alpha modulation, and functional MRI.
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia (SZ) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are associated with convergent differences in social perception relative to non-autistic, non-schizophrenia controls (NC), but divergent patterns of alterations in early visual activity. Here, we used multimodal imaging during the Guided Visual Search task to investigate the differential patterns of early visual alteration across SZ and ASD including superior colliculus (SC) and pulvinar nucleus. In Experiment 1, simultaneous eye tracking and EEG were obtained from 91 individuals (35 NC, 20 ASD, 36 SZ). Fixation-related potential (FRP) was time-locked to fixation onset. In Experiment 2, fMRI during Guided Search was obtained from a partly overlapping sample of 71 individuals (27 NC, 25 ASD, 19 SZ). In behavioral analyses, SZ was associated with significantly prolonged search time (d=.74, p=.003), which was attributable primarily to reduced mean saccade amplitude, whereas ASD was associated with a small advantage (d=.35), which was not statistically significant. In EEG analyses, SZ was associated with reduced amplitude of the FRP P1 (lambda) response (d=1.15, p<.0001) relative to NC that remained significant following control for saccade size (p<.0001), but with normal task-related modulation of background alpha activity. In contrast, ASD was associated with normal FRP amplitude and larger alpha suppression (d=.83, p=.007) that was attributable to increased alpha levels during pre-task fixation (at matched pre-onset alpha levels, d=.14, p=.66). Within SZ, P1 correlated with the MCCB composite (r=.56, p=.001). Within ASD, ADOS-2 Communication correlated with P1 (r=.51, p=.024) and with the broadband change from pre-onset to search (r=-.51, p=.030). In fMRI, SZ was associated with correlated activation reductions in the Visual1 (Sidak p<.001) and Visual2 (Sidak p=.022) networks and SC (Sidak p=.019), whereas activation was unaffected in the Dorsal Attention and Frontoparietal networks, Frontal Eye Fields and pulvinar. In ASD, activation was increased in pulvinar (Sidak p[≤].038), but unaffected elsewhere. Cortical activation patterns associated with SC activation resembled those associated with P1 generation across groups. Overall, the findings support bottom-up disturbances of visual processing in schizophrenia. In autism, pre-onset alpha was higher and task-related suppression was larger.

papers.title: Attentional prioritization enhances the accessibility of neural representations during working memory maintenance
papers.abstract: Given the limited capacity of working memory (WM), prioritization is essential for efficient information processing. Whether prioritization acts primarily at encoding, or dynamically shapes representations during maintenance, is currently unclear. Here, we employed a delayed response task and compared prioritization conditions in which the testing order of items was either known in advance or not. Behaviorally, prioritization selectively reduced guess rates and had little effect on precision. Using multivariate pattern analysis, we decoded stimulus information from EEG voltage as an index of item specific representations, and used alpha power decoding as an index of internal attention. Prioritization did not alter decodable representations during encoding. During maintenance, however, prioritization enhanced both voltage-based decoding and alpha power-based decoding for the prioritized item. Mediation analyses further revealed an indirect association between alpha-based attentional signals and behavior via voltage-based representational strength, consistent with the idea that internal attention supports performance by maintaining prioritized representations in an accessible state.

papers.title: State-Dependent Organization of Microscale Functional Circuitry in Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: Directed functional connections between individual neurons, inferred from recorded activity, reflect information routing in cortex. Yet their organization across brain states and relation to synaptic connectivity remain poorly understood. Here, we present one of the largest single-neuron-resolution directed functional circuit maps, across about 45,000 neurons in four mouse visual areas. We inferred connections from deconvolved two-photon calcium activity with CITS, a causal-inference method designed for neural time series. In co-registered electron microscopy, CITS-inferred pairs were 3.0-fold more likely to be synaptically connected than other pairs. The map's organization aligned with synaptic connectivity at areal, laminar, and cell-type levels. In low and high pupil-linked arousal, the anterolateral area (AL) had the highest intra-areal density. The strongest inter-areal pathway linked AL with the rostrolateral area. This organization held in both states, yet mean connection strength was higher in high arousal in every scan, by 9.4% on average. Finally, stronger connections linked neurons with more similar stimulus-driven predictive performance in both states.

papers.title: Distinct neurophysiological signatures of guided visual search in schizophrenia and autism: Evidence from fixation-related potentials, alpha modulation, and functional MRI.

papers.title: NED-Net: open-source software for building and refining seizure detectors during rodent EEG experiments
papers.abstract: Long-term EEG is the main readout of rodent epilepsy models, and automated detectors are usually delivered as fixed models that a laboratory cannot adapt to its own animals. NED-Net is open-source software in which annotations, rule-based detections and model proposals share one file per recording, reviewed events train the next detector, and detection runs live during acquisition, so a detector can be refined while an experiment runs. A detector built in NED-Net on one kainate mouse cohort detected 64% of 221 video-adjudicated convulsive seizures in a second cohort as delivered, and 72% of its detections on held-out recordings were seizures. Retraining on annotations made in the app, a few seconds of review per event, raised recall to 88% at 74% precision. SeizyML, a published detector, reached similar recall with three times the detections and did not improve with the same annotations. A convulsive classifier removes non-seizures and enriches convulsive events.

papers.title: Towards an understanding of injury in aortic tissue prior to actual failure: quantification of mechanically induced collagen damage using collagen hybridizing peptides
papers.abstract: The development, validation, and optimization of endovascular aortic devices require quantitative assessment of tissue damage occurring during surgical interventions. Until now, this assessment--before complete failure--has been largely unfeasible for lack of a suitable methodology. Recently developed collagen hybridizing peptides (CHPs) allow selective detection of damage to collagen, the primary load-bearing constituent of the aortic wall. However, their application in large, mechanically loaded arteries has not yet been established. Therefore, we optimized an experimental workflow for large arteries that accounts for their energy-storage function and geometrical constraints; furthermore, we have characterized the tissue's autofluorescence and selected a suitable CHP fluorophore. Specimens from a single porcine aorta were examined using uniaxial tensile testing, histological analysis, fluorescence spectral analysis, confocal microscopy, and quantitative image analysis to present collagen damage as a function of tissue stretch. The workflow detected load-induced collagen damage before tissue failure, whereas histological evaluation showed no obvious load-induced disruption. Damage scores were comparable between the undeformed control and the specimen stretched by a factor of 1.2, while specimens stretched beyond 1.2 exhibited elevated scores. This pattern corresponded to higher complication rates with excessive stent oversizing. Furthermore, the proposed protocol can be adapted for ex vivo stent deployment experiments to compare collagen damage resulting from various aortic device designs and deployment conditions. Quantitative damage metrics could inform structurally motivated constitutive material models for computational simulations of endovascular interventions. Combined with histological and structural analyses, this workflow could also help link tissue composition--or organization--to individual susceptibility to damage.

papers.title: Expanded representation and function of PDF neurons in the mosquito circadian network
papers.abstract: Female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes can transmit pathogens when they bite humans, their preferred hosts, and this host-seeking drive is tightly gated by time of day. Daily rhythms depend on the molecular clock and communication among clock neurons, yet mosquito circadian network organization remains poorly understood. Using a mosquito-specific PERIOD antibody, we mapped the putative clock network of Aedes aegypti and found that neurons expressing the neuropeptide Pigment-Dispersing Factor (PDF) make up a much larger proportion of clock neurons compared to other insects, indicating a divergent network organization. PDF neurons are required for normal rhythms across insects, but whether their importance scales with their abundance in the network is unknown. We therefore tested the functional role of this expanded PDF neuron population in mosquitoes: we show that electrically silencing Aedes aegypti PDF neurons abolished the separation of daily activity into morning and evening peaks and led to misaligned clock protein rhythms across circadian neurons, even under entraining light-dark cycles. Thus, in a network built around an unusually large PDF population, PDF neuron activity plays an outsized role in behavioral timing and network synchrony.

papers.title: Prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling promotes maladaptive plasticity of direct pathway striatal projection neurons
papers.abstract: As Parkinson's disease (PD) progresses and nigrostriatal dopamine (DA) neuron degeneration worsens, DA replacement therapies shift from restoring motor function to evoking dyskinesia. How disease progression mediates this transition remains poorly understood. Here, we optimized a 6-hydroxydopamine (6OHDA) model that reliably generates multiple severities of DA axon denervation within the striatum of individual mice. We identify a critical denervation threshold at which direct-pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs), which are key drivers of dyskinesia become pathologically hyperresponsive to DA. Using slice electrophysiology, we establish that denervation-induced increase in intrinsic excitability is insufficient to explain the aberrant response of dSPNs to DA. We further demonstrate using genetic and chemogenetic manipulations that prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling drives the pathological transformation of dSPNs cell-autonomously, and that sustained Gs-coupled metabotropic receptor signaling in dSPNs is sufficient to both prevent and reverse it. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how PD progression renders striatal circuits vulnerable to DA-evoked motor complications and identify sustained signaling by Gs-coupled receptors as a potential avenue for preventing or reversing denervation-induced maladaptive striatal plasticity.

papers.title: WITHDRAWN: Identifying Phelan-McDermid-Like Electrophysiological Subtypes in Autism Using EEG and Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The authors have withdrawn this manuscript until a re-evaluation of the clinical data is completed. Therefore, the authors do not wish this work to be cited as reference for the project. If you have any questions, please contact the corresponding author.

papers.title: Local and network-level dynamics of alpha and beta rhythms during visuospatial attention in autism
papers.abstract: Visuospatial attention is altered in autism, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Neural oscillatory activity coordinates distributed processes supporting attentional selection and their flexible adjustment to changing environmental demands. Altered oscillatory organization may therefore provide a mechanistic basis for atypical attentional processing in autism. We tested this theory using EEG recordings from 80 autistic and neurotypical children and youth performing a spatial cueing task with valid and invalid cues. We quantified alpha- and beta-band measures of local power and inter-trial phase clustering (ITPC) together with power- and phase-based measures of posterior-frontal long-range connectivity. Across validity conditions, autistic participants showed a more frontal alpha distribution, reduced posterior alpha lateralization and posterior beta ITPC, and higher frontal beta power. Crucially, autistic participants also presented reduced neural adaptation across attentional conditions, reflected in attenuated validity-dependent modulation of alpha power and of posterior-frontal beta connectivity, with elevated beta connectivity particularly in the valid cue condition. This neural pattern was accompanied by greater reaction-time slowing in the invalid compared with the valid cue condition. Within autistic participants, beta dynamics showed nominal associations with restricted and repetitive behaviors that did not survive multiple-comparison correction. Together, these findings suggest that visuospatial attention in autism is characterized by altered local oscillatory organization, combined with reduced modulation of local and distributed dynamics as attentional demands change. Alterations in alpha and beta activity may reflect reduced spatially selective attentional gating alongside greater maintenance of established attentional states.

papers.title: Shox2 maintains thalamocortical neuron firing for whisker-based somatomotor responses and sleep spindles in mice
papers.abstract: In the mouse thalamus, thalamocortical neurons (TCNs) relay sensory information to cortex and generate rhythmic activity, including sleep spindles, through precisely timed firing. TCNs switch between tonic and burst firing modes that depend on intrinsic membrane properties, yet what maintains these properties in the mature thalamus remains unknown. Transcription factors, which regulate the ion channel genes that shape firing, are natural candidates. Here, we investigate Shox2, a transcription factor implicated in rhythmic activity across multiple systems, in ventral posterior medial (VPM) thalamus. Using genetic labeling and optogenetic activation, we show that Shox2 expressing neurons form functional thalamocortical and thalamoreticular projections capable of driving cortical responses. Conditional knockout of Shox2 in VPM alters intrinsic membrane properties, reducing both tonic and burst firing without altering thalamocortical circuit organization or barrel field architecture. These firing deficits are accompanied by impaired whisker-dependent somatomotor performance and a reduction in sleep spindle density in cortical target regions, while overall sleep architecture remains intact. Together, these findings identify Shox2 as a transcriptional regulator required to maintain intrinsic firing modes in VPM thalamocortical neurons, linking a transcription factor to spindle deficits, an emerging neurophysiological biomarker for autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia.

papers.title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
papers.abstract: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

papers.title: Longitudinal computer vision-based behavioural phenotyping of group-housed dogs for translational and welfare research
papers.abstract: Continuous behavioural monitoring is essential for assessing animal welfare and individual behavioural variation, yet traditional observation-based methods are labour-intensive and prone to bias. Here, we developed a modular framework with computer vision for automated behavioural profiling of group-housed Beagles, integrating You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based models for pose estimation, individual identification, and enrichment detection. A ceiling-mounted infrared camera system enabled uninterrupted monitoring under standard kennel conditions. The identity-independent YOLO-POSE model achieved 99% precision, 97% recall, and an mAP50 of 0.98, while the YOLO classification model reached 95% accuracy for individual identification without external markers. Combining posture, identity, and environmental information enabled automated quantification of spatial use, locomotor activity, social interactions, corridor-oriented behaviour, drinking behaviour, and enrichment use. Overall, this framework captured distinct behavioural profiles of individual dogs from the same litter housed in the same kennel, which can be used to assess animal welfare and to evaluate environmental enrichments objectively. Together, we demonstrate a scalable and non-invasive approach for continuous individual behavioural profiling of group-housed dogs for computational ethology and translational research. By separating pose estimation from identity assignment, the framework enables flexible deployment across changing social groups and facilitates application to previously unseen individuals with minimal training.

papers.title: FUSE: FUsing EEG-MEG in a Shared Embedding via self-supervised learning for BCI
papers.abstract: Combining complementary neurophysiological modalities offers a promising strategy for improving motor imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), but learning shared representations across modalities remains largely unexplored. Here, we propose a two-phase deep learning framework for multimodal EEG-MEG decoding that explicitly decouples representation learning from downstream classification. In the first phase, a convolutional encoder-decoder learns a shared latent representation by predicting the power spectral density (PSD) of EEG and MEG signals directly from time-domain activity, rather than using the conventional objective of reconstructing the input signal. In the second phase, the encoder is frozen and its learned representations are reused, without further adaptation, to perform the classification of the downstream MI-BCI task. The framework was evaluated on simultaneous EEG and MEG recordings from 20 participants. The learned representations consistently outperformed conventional handcrafted spectral features, increasing median classification accuracy from 0.734 to 0.794. The multimodal framework also improved performance over MEG alone (median accuracy from 0.680 to 0.794) and yielded a modest increase over EEG alone (median accuracy from 0.765 to 0.794), providing a more robust decoding strategy than single-modality approaches. Furthermore, the learned latent representations were transferable across participants, with more than half of cross-subject models performing within 0.01 accuracy of their subject-specific counterparts. These findings demonstrate that task-agnostic representation learning can capture physiologically meaningful multimodal neural representations that remain transferable across individuals, offering a promising foundation for more robust and reusable BCI pipelines.

papers.title: MLE EEG Toolbox: A Personal AI Laboratory Assistant for Literature-Informed and Reproducible M/EEG Research
papers.abstract: Electrophysiological research increasingly relies on complex analytical workflows, yet integrating methodological evidence, computational execution and reproducibility remains challenging. Here we introduce MLE EEG Toolbox, a framework for building a personal AI laboratory assistant for electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) research. The toolbox integrates locally deployed AI, natural-language-guided analysis, literature retrieval and methodological comparison, and reproducible computational workflows. A constrained language model translates research instructions into validated, researcher-approved operations, while literature-informed guidance supports parameter selection and protocol reconstruction. Computational provenance enables transparent inspection and replay of analytical workflows. The assistant achieved action-selection accuracies of 85.6% for EEG and 95.5% for MEG, while 142 cross-platform tests demonstrated close numerical agreement. Applications to public EEG and MEG datasets illustrated integrated spectral, network, decoding and source analyses. Running on standard personal computers without external AI APIs or token charges, MLE EEG Toolbox provides an accessible, researcher-controlled environment that connects methodological knowledge with reproducible electrophysiological analysis.

papers.title: Early Life Shift in Fear Extinction is Driven by Prefrontal-Amygdala Engagement
papers.abstract: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) displays a delayed maturation long hypothesized to guide developmental changes in threat processing. Nevertheless, the mechanism by which ontogenetic changes in mPFC function guide the developmental emergence of behavior is unclear. Early life marks a shift between a permanent extinction phenotype typical of juveniles, toward the standard, more transient extinction seen in adult rodents. This shift coincides with developmental changes in mPFC-amygdala connectivity, a pathway necessary for extinction processing in adults. Here we used optogenetics and slice electrophysiology to show that, in contrast to adult animals, juvenile mice displaying permanent extinction fail to engage the mPFC-amygdala pathway at the synaptic, cell activity or behavioral levels. Consistent with a requirement of this pathway for the developmental transition in extinction types, optic potentiation of the mPFC-amygdala pathway accelerates the onset of adult extinction. Our findings show that the developmental onboarding of the mPFC-amygdala pathway drives a shift in extinction processing toward increased fear reemergence that persists throughout adulthood.

papers.title: From clusters to curves: A model-based alternative to cluster-based permutation tests for the analysis of time-resolved data
papers.abstract: Time-resolved electrophysiological measurements such as those obtained through magneto- and electroencephalography (M/EEG) offer a unique window onto the neural activity underlying cognitive processes. Researchers are often interested in determining whether and when these signals differ across experimental conditions or participant groups. The conventional approach involves mass univariate statistical testing across time and space followed by corrections for multiple comparisons or some form of cluster-based inference. While effective for controlling error rates at the cluster-level, cluster-based inference comes with a significant limitation: by shifting the focus of inference from individual time points to clusters, it prevents drawing conclusions about the precise onset or offset of observed effects. Here, we present a model-based alternative for analysing M/EEG time series, such as event-related potentials or time-resolved decoding accuracy. Our approach leverages Bayesian generalised additive multilevel models, providing posterior odds at each time point, while naturally accounting for between-participant variability. Using simulated data with known ground truth, we show that the proposed approach consistently provides accurate recovery of the overall temporal extent and onset of neural effects across a range of signal-to-noise ratios, although offset localisation is comparatively more variable. In an empirical MEG decoding dataset, the approach also yields the highest split-half temporal overlap among the methods considered and highly stable temporal segmentation across repeated participant splits. Together, these results illustrate the potential of model-based inference as a complementary approach to conventional cluster-based procedures when temporally localised inference and explicit modelling of between-participant variability are scientifically important. We provide an open-source R package implementing the method and describe how it can be integrated into M/EEG analysis pipelines using MNE-Python.
